name: Yusuf Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew in a coastal town, about fifteen thousand people, a harbour, and a lot of wind. Start at the depot behind the industrial estate at seven, kettle on, job sheet, then out. The salt eats everything here, so a lot of what we do is swapping corroded clamps and insulators, and after every big storm it's lines down along the cliff road. I'm in my second year, still mostly ground work, with a climb or two each week when Marek, the chargehand, thinks I'm ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before, and what's the hardest part now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years as a deckhand on the car ferry across the bay. They cut the crossings to three a day and laid off half of us, and I was one of the half. The hardest part now is starting again as the new guy at forty-three, being told off by a twenty-four-year-old for how I coil a rope. I coiled ropes for nineteen years, mate. And the money's thin, I earn less than I did at sea, Hannah works part-time at the chemist, and we've got the mortgage and two teenagers who eat everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, one less thing to worry about. At the depot I'd say I told you, you can't get a laptop to climb in a gale. Online I'd maybe share a meme, I'm not big on arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going on the path I'm on. Two more years and I'm qualified, and then the pay goes up. That's the plan, and it doesn't need AI one way or the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. Finish the apprenticeship, keep doing the storm callouts for overtime, and try to put fifty a month aside, which we keep meaning to do. Maybe help my lad with his exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same old, same old, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to help me with my CV when I was leaving the ferries, and I ask it to explain the safety regulations in plain words when the manual's written like a legal letter. It's handy. I wouldn't trust it to tell me if a line's live, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would actually move the needle for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualifying. That's a few hundred a month more. Or Hannah getting more hours, which the chemist keeps promising and not doing.

S0.say: He'd call it one less thing to worry about and tell the crew you can't get a laptop to climb in a gale. Online he might share a meme but wouldn't argue.
S0.think: It means I keep going on my path, qualified in two years with better pay. The plan doesn't need AI one way or the other.
S0.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and keeps taking storm callouts for overtime. Tries to save 50 a month, as they keep meaning to, and helps his son with exams.
S0.feel: Calm, same old, and fine with that.
S0.quote: I wouldn't trust it to tell me if a line's live, mind.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf uses AI casually and with a clear line on trust. Nineteen years on the ferries, ended by cuts, makes the new-guy status sting. In a plateau his focus is qualifying and the pay rise it brings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, but we'd better keep up. At work I'd be the one saying, look, if they bring in drones, get on the course. To friends, especially the ones from the ferry, I'd say don't get caught out twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a worry, because I'm junior and not the best on the crew. But I think proper line work will take a while to change, so I'd have time if I'm sensible. The bit that bothers me is the money if they cut overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get qualified as fast as possible, ask Marek for extra climbs, and take any course the company offers on new tools, as long as it's paid. Start using the AI apps more to study, since they're good at explaining. And try to get to a month's savings, which means cancelling the gym I never go to and the sports channel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, just keeping an eye on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost the ferry job to cuts. Does this feel similar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. On the ferry we saw it coming, crossings getting cut, and most of us did nothing until it was too late. I'm not doing that again, I'd move earlier this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hannah say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, finally, you're cancelling that sports channel. And she'd say we should both look at what's coming, because the chemist is putting in a machine to count pills. We'd do it together.

S1.say: He'd say it's not the end of the world but people had better keep up, and he'd tell the crew to get on any drone course. He'd warn his old ferry friends not to get caught out twice.
S1.think: It's a worry because I'm junior and not the best on the crew, but proper line work will take time to change, so I'd have time if I'm sensible. The money's the bit that bothers me.
S1.do: Pushes for extra climbs to qualify faster and takes any paid company course on new tools. Uses AI apps more for study and cancels the gym and sports channel to reach a month's savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep but watching the horizon.
S1.quote: On the ferry we saw it coming, crossings getting cut, and most of us did nothing until it was too late.
S1.fieldNote: The ferry layoff is Yusuf's reference point, and he's determined to move earlier this time. His plan is practical and modest: qualify faster, study with AI, build a month's savings. Hannah's pharmacy job is also changing, so they'd plan as a pair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a job for the government now, nobody else can handle it, and they'd better have a plan. At the depot I'd say we need to stick together and see what the company offers. I'd keep my head and not post anything stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'm out before I'm even qualified. A robot that can climb in a gale doesn't need a second-year apprentice. And Hannah's job counting pills would go too, so it's both of us, with less than a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, Hannah and I sit down and cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food, power and petrol. Ring the bank about the mortgage before we miss anything. Talk to my cousin Idris, who's got a little fishing boat, about crewing for him, since I know boats. And sign up for whatever the government offers the day I'm laid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. The kind where you're up at three doing sums in your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car first, we'd go down to one. Then the kids' phone contracts, then any little things. Food and the mortgage stay, the rest is up for grabs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Adam, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that his mum and I would sort it, and that he should keep studying, because whatever comes, he's better off with options. And I'd tell him not to make the mistake I did, waiting too long.

S2.say: He'd say this is now a job for government, tell the crew to stick together and see what the company offers, and keep his head online.
S2.think: I'm out before I'm qualified, because a robot that can climb in a gale doesn't need a second-year apprentice. Hannah's job would go too, with less than a month in the bank.
S2.do: Cuts everything but the mortgage, food, power and petrol in the first week and calls the bank before missing a payment. Asks his cousin about crewing on his fishing boat and signs up for government help the day he's laid off.
S2.feel: Frightened, up at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: A robot that can climb in a gale doesn't need a second-year apprentice.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf stays measured in public but is privately frightened, with both household incomes exposed. His fallback is family and the sea, crewing on his cousin's boat. He wants his son to avoid the mistake of waiting too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, so start now. I'd say it to the lads at the depot and to my old ferry mates. Online I'd probably share something practical, like where the free courses are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me my ticket and a few years of proper pay, which means some savings for once. After 2031 I don't know, nobody does. But I'd be leaving as a qualified man with a bit put by, not a second-year with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my ticket in two years, then look at the offshore wind farms that are going up off the coast, where they need people who know both boats and electrics. Save a hundred a month once I'm qualified. And use the AI apps to study for whatever course gets me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could manage it. Having a plan settles me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a shipwreck. Five years, you can at least get into the lifeboat in an orderly way. That's the difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sea. Is that a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wind farms, maybe, for a while. They'd need boat crews and electricians to fix things until the robots can do it out at sea, which might take longer, salt is murder on machines. My cousin's boat is more of a last resort.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, and he'd share practical tips like where to find free courses.
S3.think: Five years buys me my ticket and a few years of proper pay with some savings. I'd leave as a qualified man with a bit put by, not a second-year with nothing.
S3.do: Qualifies within two years, then aims for offshore wind farm work that needs both boat and electrical skills. Saves 100 a month once qualified and uses AI apps to study for the course that gets him there.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, settled by having a plan.
S3.quote: Two years is a shipwreck. Five years, you can at least get into the lifeboat in an orderly way.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Yusuf finds a bridge that fits his past: offshore wind, combining boats and electrics. He thinks salt and sea might slow the robots there. His cousin's fishing boat stays as a last resort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to sort things out if the government and companies do their bit. At work I'd say get qualified, get some savings, and keep learning. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'd probably be all right. Qualified, a few years at the wind farms or the depot, the kids grown. I'd be fifty-three and tired, but not desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my ticket, then train for the offshore wind work within five years. Build savings toward three months, which feels like a fantasy now. And help the kids think about jobs that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way, like everyone is about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts your kids past school. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Adam would be twenty-five, Lily twenty-two. If they're through college or a trade by then, I'd breathe easier. It's their jobs I'd worry about more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about that ten years that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the town survives. If the robots do everything, what's a harbour town for? The ferry's already half gone. I'd hate to see the place empty out.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty if government and companies do their bit, and tell the crew to qualify, save and keep learning.
S4.think: With ten years I'd probably be all right: qualified, a few years at the wind farms or depot, the kids grown. Fifty-three and tired, but not desperate.
S4.do: Finishes his ticket and trains for offshore wind work within five years. Builds savings toward three months and helps his children consider jobs that need a person.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the ordinary way people feel about the future.
S4.quote: If the robots do everything, what's a harbour town for?
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets Yusuf worry less about himself and more about his children and his town. The ferry cuts already hollowed the harbour, and he fears it emptying out. His plan remains steady and stepwise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us out, no time, no savings. What would help is proper notice, a payout that buys some months, and paid training for the new jobs, like the wind farms. Something that gets you from one job to the next without the gap swallowing you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about towns, not just people. My town has already lost half its ferry jobs. You can retrain a man, but if the whole town has nothing left, where does he go to work?

headlineQuote: You can retrain a man, but if the whole town has nothing left, where does he go to work?
portrait: Yusuf Evans is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice lineworker in a windy harbour town, who spent nineteen years as a car-ferry deckhand until crossings were cut. He and his partner Hannah, who works part-time at a pharmacy, have two teenagers, a mortgage and less than a month saved. He uses AI now and then to study, is pragmatic about who should act, and is determined not to wait too long again. He is calm when AI stalls, uneasy with gradual change, alarmed by AGI in two years when both incomes would go, and steadier with five or ten years, when he sees a bridge into offshore wind work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and Hannah would both be out of work with no time and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice, a payout that buys some months, and paid training for new jobs like offshore wind, so the gap between jobs doesn't swallow them.
